In investigating graduate education, you might ask yourself, 'what do I want to study,' or 'what am I interested in.' And they might seem to be principle questions, the gateway beyond which lies any meaningful higher education. But graduate education, as I've come to see it (and the progress of the world around it), no longer obeys a 'principle of interest;' that interests are singular and are formed at some early period and extend through a career and lifetime. Even outside of the crisis of attention'which I would propose results from the emphasis, both financial and as a function of our biological circuitry, on shorter and shorter forms of media AND the increasing burden of media on our consciousness'there are no longer even clear fields of study. The giants of the past (particle physics comes to mind) have grinded to a halt or have been diluted into infinitesimal tributaries of fractal niches. But perhaps that is the natural course of the sciences. To dive deeper and deeper is to accept higher and more fundamental levels of complexity and interconnectedness. But how, as a curious, driven young person, can you enter from the opposite side of those tributaries. How can you begin to decide a path when the path begins twenty years down a very narrow hall, where the questions themselves barely have room to breathe. You might make a decision based on the bouncing of terms of art off your tongue. Seems as reasonable a method as any when the alternative is to sift though tens of thousands of articles published in thousands of journals (with extremely muddy financial ethics), and hoping by an act of god to distill some useful framework.

The anxiety of a certain relation seems/feels completely overwhelming at some moments. I think about the science of arousal (Gustafsson E, Ib'ez de Aldecoa P, Burdett ERR. A shared 'optimal-level of arousal': Seeking basis for creativity and curiosity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences. 2024;47:e100. doi:10.1017/S0140525X23003552) in this context; the anxiety/burden aggravates in the mind an arousal that opposes the creative intention. And induces, subsequently, a resentment poisonous to the relationship and feeds into a vicious loops through which such anxiety and resentment proliferate. At the root of this is 'continuous' communication. Characterizes by forms such as text messages, where a communication sits awaiting response as opposed to a more 'natural' communication, where messages are addressed in the immediate. Actually, communication in this latter form, may also generate anxiety as a product of un-response, but generally to a lesser degree. The un-response anxiety is not limited to the person sending communication. The person receiving communication may, just as easily, foster this in-response anxiety. And I would argue that it is unfair to claim that such anxiety is wholly the product of their own non-response, in spite of the fact that they do, in one sense, have the means to alleviate this tension. One such reason, getting back to the idea of 'continuous' communication (I'm focusing principally on text messaging), is that the barrier to entry for such communication is inherently lower; there does not need to be a mutual agreement to engage in conversation as there does (for the most part) in more 'natural' communications. So, while it may feel to the sender of the message that the un-response is a slight, they must be aware of the fact that there is no implicit agreement in this kind of communication (except, of course, if there is). Additionally, I would claim that the source of the such anxiety is more fundamentally the result of communal breakdown. The necessity of continuous forms of communication is the result of a more physically splintered society (which, I would add, is a bit paradoxical given the growing size and population of city centers [this is a more anecdotal conceit]), which can no longer depend stochastic meetings as result of shared living or working spaces nor can it depend on the ease of such meetings outside of chance encounters. It may also be the case, to return to the idea of anxiety/resentment loops, that such loops, driven by a breakdown in communal structure may also exist within a larger loop that perpetuates such societal splintering; that an increasing number of interpersonal relations flirt with such anxiety/resentment loops may drive individuals towards isolation and this isolation fuels further anxiety and resentment. At some point, individuals sever relational ties so severely that they must conclude that relationships are, by their nature, fueled by anxiety and resentment. I suppose another way of articulating all this is, that the overwhelming proportion of positive relational benefits are received in the so-called 'natural' communication, and one would do best to organize their life around ease of this communication in favor of the 'continuous' kind.

I also believe that ignorance is liberating, and I find muddling through to be extremely satisfying. He's also dead-on about how poorly students are prepared for research (there's a huge caveat there though because an undergraduate education is not at all tuned toward preparing students for original research, probably because the incentives are simply not there). And not just poorly prepared for research but almost willfully misinformed about what it is. That aside, I think he's missing a huge piece here; I don't think his friend left academia solely because she was uncomfortable bumbling around in the unknown. The interesting thing for me is how different personalities within science digest and project the dichotomy of knowing nothing with the prestige of a research position. It was quickly apparent to me that no one in the lab had some terrifying intellect (and that's not to say they weren't extremely talented), and it was also clear that the significance of the research amounted more to contributing to a relatively abstract pool of knowledge, whose real applications were tenuous (that's probably highly debatable, but the research was almost certainly more piecewise than translational), than paradigm-shifting. Despite that, the unknown of it all creates a huge vacuum (it is literally a vacuum), which paired with the hierarchical construction of university or research institution, requires assertion of knowledge from the top down. It was not the scope of the research problems or the infinite void of unknowledge that made me feel stupid. It was the other researchers. It was posturing and tone of voice and trust not given. It was the safeguarding of knowledge for the understanding that it was incomplete, that it would always be incomplete, and for the fear that that knowledge might be better utilized, more creatively interpreted by someone else.
